source_title: Sample Podcast: Off-Grid Power and the Pay-As-You-Go Model
text:
Host: Today I'm speaking with Thabo Molefe, who founded SolaraGrid. Thabo, welcome.

Thabo Molefe: Thank you for having me.

Host: SolaraGrid started in 2015, is that right?

Thabo Molefe: We registered the company in Johannesburg in June 2015, though I had been running it out of a garage in Soweto for about a year before that. My background is electrical engineering. I studied at the University of Cape Town and then spent six years at a utility, which is where I formed the view that the grid was never going to reach the last fifteen percent of households on any timeline that mattered.

Host: What was the first product?

Thabo Molefe: A solar home system. A panel, a battery, three lights and a phone charger. Nothing novel about the hardware. The novel part was that we did not sell it. We leased it, and the customer paid by mobile money in daily increments of around twelve rand. If they stopped paying, the unit locked itself remotely until they resumed. That pay-as-you-go model is what made it work, because the barrier was never that people did not want power, it was that nobody could put down four thousand rand at once.

Host: How many households now?

Thabo Molefe: We passed three hundred thousand connected households in 2023, across South Africa, Zambia and Mozambique. Zambia is now our fastest growing market.

Host: You had a serious crisis in 2019. Can you talk about it?

Thabo Molefe: Yes, and I think it is the most useful thing I can tell anyone. In 2019 our default rate went from about six percent to nineteen percent in a single quarter. We nearly did not survive it. The instinct in the room was that we had a credit problem and needed to tighten who we sold to. That instinct was wrong. When we actually went and sat in customers' homes, we found the defaults clustered almost entirely around units that had been installed by one particular subcontractor in Limpopo whose installations were failing after about eight months. People were not refusing to pay. They were refusing to pay for a light that did not turn on.

Host: So it was an operations problem wearing a finance problem's clothes.

Thabo Molefe: Exactly that. We brought installation fully in-house in 2020, and default came back down to seven percent within three quarters. It cost us more per installation and it was unambiguously the right call. I now believe that in this business the person who screws the bracket to the roof matters more than the person who builds the financing model.

Host: What about the carbon credit side?

Thabo Molefe: We started registering our deployments for carbon credits in 2021. It is real revenue, roughly eleven percent of turnover last year, but I am careful about it. I have watched companies build their entire model on credit pricing and then get destroyed when methodologies were revised. We treat it as a bonus on top of a business that has to work without it.

Host: What is next?

Thabo Molefe: Productive use. A light and a phone charger changes a household. A solar-powered irrigation pump or a refrigeration unit changes a household's income. We began piloting agricultural pumps in Zambia in 2024 with about nine hundred units. That is where I think the next decade of this sector actually is.
